evidence.text: The fixed inventory lists 229 substantive written pieces from 15 outlets. This game selects four outlets and derives their daily counts from its dated rows.

evidence.text: 24 July to 14 August 2026, ending at 15:12 BST. Passing mentions, broadcasts and video-only items are excluded. Coverage of indexing gaps is qualified.

evidence.label: Resignation report, 5 August
evidence.text: Arday resigned from his Cambridge role on 5 August.

evidence.label: Independent inquiry report, 12 August
evidence.text: Cambridge agreed to an independent inquiry into his appointment on 12 August.

evidence.label: Arday’s resignation statement, 5 August
evidence.text: Arday said public scrutiny had taken a toll on his family. He said resigning should not be read as acceptance of the narratives about him.

evidence.label: Denial reported with resignation
evidence.text: Arday denied plagiarism.

evidence.label: Early commentary, 30 July
evidence.text: An early commentator acknowledged that the plagiarism question remained unresolved and focused criticism on Cambridge’s appointment checks.

evidence.label: Leading article in the 8 August issue
evidence.text: A leading article used the Arday affair to argue that Cambridge and universities had sacrificed academic standards to progressive politics.

evidence.label: Commentary published 10 August
evidence.text: A later commentary invoked fictional impostors and connected Arday’s case to a broader attack on diversity, equity and inclusion.

evidence.label: Investigation published 1 August
evidence.text: Reporting questioned accounts of alleged racist threats.

evidence.label: Varsity’s firsthand reporting, September 2023
evidence.text: Varsity reported an upheld complaint concerning student essays copied into William O’Reilly’s journal article. It reported a negligence finding, a withdrawn article and his return to work. Cambridge’s full tribunal reasons were not published.

evidence.label: Columnist’s comparison, August 2026
evidence.text: Columnist Jason Okundaye estimated roughly six press articles about O’Reilly. He supplied no matching window or counting method.

evidence.label: First report and responses, 1 August
evidence.text: Current page checked 13 October 2026. Its headline includes his defence. The body presents his response, an allegation originator’s background, conflicting academic views and a warning from Simon Baron-Cohen about the effect of continuing scrutiny. It also uses wording that he did not dispute allegations. This is a tension to examine alongside his later explicit denial, not proof that every version or report omitted his response.

evidence.label: Institutional analysis, 6 August
evidence.text: Current page checked 13 October 2026. The analysis connects appointment checks with an institutional diversity agenda. It also records Arday’s denial and the university union’s concern about fair process and Black underrepresentation. A policy inference should be tested against the actual evidence, including these counterarguments.

evidence.label: Cancelled event and remaining roles, 10 August
evidence.text: Current page checked 13 October 2026. It reports a cancelled appearance and a further association resignation, checks several continuing roles, and repeats Arday’s statement about the toll of scrutiny. The presence of developments does not by itself settle the justification for pursuing every role.

evidence.label: Version and inventory limits
evidence.text: The fixed written inventory and selected current pages do not provide a complete archive of changes, a full broadcast census, a novelty classification or a matched comparator. Missing search results do not prove no coverage; a changed or removed page does not alone establish a cover-up.

evidence.label: Opinion defending diversity, 13 August
evidence.text: A selected opinion headline argues for defending diversity. This adds a different perspective but remains another publication drawing attention to the same case. It does not establish the tone or value of all eighteen pieces.

evidence.label: Original Cambridge statement, 12 August 2026
evidence.text: Cambridge announced an independent appointment investigation. Its statement also affirmed that staff of colour were valued and this case should not be generalised to them. This was an announcement, not an investigation finding.

briefing.title: We must defend our widening coverage

paragraphs.text: We would defend reporting allegations about a prominent university appointment, while preserving the distinction between questions and findings. Our first listed report, on the first of August, put Arday’s defence in its headline. It described the source of the allegations and carried opposing academic views. But its wording about not disputing allegations deserves scrutiny alongside his later explicit denial. We cannot let repeated reporting flatten those distinctions.

After the resignation on the fifth, the story moved into separate institutional responses. On the sixth, the Met commissioner accepted a mistake over investigating a journalist. The next day brought Cambridge and Glasgow appointment reviews. Belfast then looked into co-authored work. By the twelfth, Cambridge had confirmed an independent investigation. Those developments can explain renewed interest, but none was a final finding against Arday.

Nine written pieces are listed, with two on each of our busiest dates. The current Cambridge report already mentions Glasgow’s review, while a separate Glasgow-focused report appeared that evening. Without their earlier versions, we cannot say exactly what the later piece added. On the tenth, a cancelled appearance and BSA resignation were reported alongside checks on other roles. We must defend both the information and the scale of that attention, especially after an earlier report carried a warning about continued scrutiny.

The earlier O’Reilly case is a useful consistency question, but not a settled numerical comparison. Varsity reported the tribunal outcome, and we have now linked another original interview with him. Neither that recovery nor a columnist’s rough estimate is a matched census. The cases also differed in stage: one had a tribunal outcome, while this window contained allegations and new inquiries. We would need equally complete records before defending a precise difference in attention.

coverageNotes.text: We would defend reporting allegations about a prominent university appointment, while preserving the distinction between questions and findings. Our first listed report, on the first of August, put Arday’s defence in its headline. It described the source of the allegations and carried opposing academic views. But its wording about not disputing allegations deserves scrutiny alongside his later explicit denial. We cannot let repeated reporting flatten those distinctions.

After his resignation on the fifth, our coverage continued into institutional responses. Our analysis the next day connected appointment checks with diversity policy, while also carrying the union’s counterargument. On the tenth, we reported a cancelled appearance and another association resignation, and checked other roles. By the twelfth, an independent appointment inquiry supplied a further development. These were different developments, but that does not automatically justify every part of the follow-up.

We owe you an answer about proportion. Nine written pieces are listed, with two on each of our busiest dates. Our first report had already carried a warning about the effect of continuing scrutiny. Arday later described the toll on his family. What public need did tracking the remaining roles serve, and could we have explained institutional responsibility with less personal exposure? Those are fair challenges to our editorial choices.

The earlier O’Reilly complaint also tests consistency. Its quieter coverage is a columnist’s estimate, not a matched census. And our nine written pieces exclude broadcasts; they cannot be compared directly with a broader pages-and-programmes tally. We would need a complete record of our attention and significant edits to defend the campaign as a whole.

briefing.title: We investigated claims and challenged the wider backlash

paragraphs.text: We would defend this campaign as both investigation and a debate about its wider consequences. On the first of August, reporting questioned accounts of alleged racist threats. Four days later, Arday resigned from Cambridge. He denied plagiarism and said stepping down was not acceptance of the narratives about him. Those responses matter alongside the allegations.

Eighteen of our pieces are listed. There were four on the sixth of August, four the following day and another four on the twelfth, when the appointment inquiry was announced. Selected opinion headlines defended diversity. Our case is that readers needed both scrutiny of the university and a challenge to arguments treating one contested case as a verdict on racial equality.

But that does not make every additional piece necessary. Investigations, opinion columns and letters all add to the attention focused on the same person. Even supportive commentary can prolong that spotlight. We must defend the amount of new understanding our campaign offered, as well as the merits of any one article.

A quieter Cambridge case gives you a question to put to us. Varsity reported that a plagiarism complaint against historian William O’Reilly was upheld, with a negligence finding, and that he returned to work. A columnist estimated much less press coverage. We cannot dismiss the consistency question. But we also cannot turn that rough estimate into a proven comparison: there is no matching inventory, and the cases were at different stages. Ask us why those differences would justify the scale of attention here.

briefing.title: We treated this as an argument about institutional standards

paragraphs.text: Our defence starts with Cambridge, rather than a final finding against Arday. An early commentary on the thirtieth of July acknowledged that the plagiarism question remained unresolved. It challenged the university’s appointment checks. We would argue that an institution’s decisions deserve scrutiny while allegations against an individual are still being examined.

Then the campaign broadened. Five of our pieces are listed on the fifth of August, the date Arday resigned. Our leading article argued that the affair exposed wider problems with academic standards and progressive politics. Five more pieces are listed on the tenth. One commentary used fictional impostors to make an argument against diversity, equity and inclusion. That was political opinion; it was not a new tribunal finding.

Twenty-one pieces are listed altogether, with ten concentrated on those two dates. We would defend commentary that explains why a university controversy matters beyond one appointment. But we owe you evidence for that wider argument. One contested case cannot establish the merit of whole groups, and repeating a political judgment does not make it better supported.

Arday denied plagiarism and said scrutiny had taken a toll on his family. Your challenge to us is whether this intensity kept adding something the public needed, or whether our commentary became a succession of opportunities to rehearse the same argument at his expense.

The O’Reilly comparison can test consistency, but its quieter coverage is a columnist’s estimate, not an equivalent article count. It should prompt a question to us, rather than decide the answer for you.

briefing.title: We kept asking questions after the resignation

paragraphs.text: We would defend sustained attention because resignation did not answer the questions about Cambridge’s appointment or the accuracy of public claims. Our first listed report appeared on the twenty-fourth of July, framing a plagiarism row around a much-publicised appointment. Later headings moved into Arday’s memoir, the university’s hiring decisions and wider political criticism. That widening agenda is central to the case you should put to us.

Arday resigned on the fifth of August. He denied plagiarism and said scrutiny had taken a toll on his family. The next two dates were our busiest: seven listed pieces on the sixth and seven on the seventh. Thirty pieces fall on or after the resignation date. The archive lists forty-two altogether, making this the most sustained campaign among the four outlets in this round.

Our argument is that public claims and institutional responsibility can remain news after a person leaves their job. But that is a reason to investigate further, not a blank cheque for the volume we published. You should ask which later pieces uncovered something important, which explained developments, and which mainly repeated an established criticism. The listed headings suggest different themes, but cannot prove that every article added fresh evidence.

A comparison with William O’Reilly raises the question of consistency. Varsity documented an upheld complaint, a negligence finding and a withdrawn article. A columnist described much quieter attention, without a matching count or period. We would have to explain why the differences between the cases warranted our intensity here. We cannot simply say that a serious allegation makes any amount of coverage proportionate.

sequence.text: The selected inventory begins with reporting on a plagiarism row.
Investigative coverage questioned accounts of alleged racist threats; other written coverage carried his defence.
Arday resigned and described the personal toll, while rejecting acceptance of the narratives.
An independent inquiry into his appointment was agreed.

context.allegationResponse: Arday denied plagiarism. His resignation should not be treated as a finding of guilt.

title: Caroline Flack: recovered dated headline sample
subject: Public coverage of Caroline Flack from the assault charge through 14 February 2020
endNote: Inclusive sample window; ends before later coverage of Flack’s death.

source.name: Dated publisher and archive records; separate Guardian aggregate
source.scopeNote: Fixed window 2019-12-12 through 2020-02-14 inclusive. Counts derive only from 32 dated recovered headlines across 8 outlets; the chart selects 4 desks and 26 records. Missing records/dates are not proof nothing was published; this is not a census and counts do not establish motive, harm or causation.
source.sampleNote: 32 dated rows across 8 outlets; selected chart desks are Independent, ITV, Guardian and Sun (26 recovered records, not a census). MailOnline is included in the full sample but not the playable chart. Exact headline/date provenance varies by live publisher metadata or archived capture; publication, update and capture dates are distinct.

events.label: Charged with assault by beating
Stepped down from Love Island hosting
Laura Whitmore confirmed as replacement host
Posted that this was the worst time of her life on eve of court appearance
Pleaded not guilty; bail conditions remained; trial set for March 2020
Christmas message: said she was taking a social-media break and was not going to be silenced
Lewis Burton denied that blood shown in bedroom photos was his.
Relationship-breakup reports were challenged; Flack objected to her family's life being treated as entertainment or gossip
The Sun published an online Valentine-card story later removed/replaced

evidence.label: Guardian aggregate and method
evidence.text: The Guardian reports 387 print stories across UK national newspapers and 99 Sun stories mentioning Flack. Inclusion was her name in headline or body during 14 Aug 2019–14 Feb 2020. Three journalists classified tone; the article says the analysis is not definitive. Most stories were neutral overall; December negative headlines rose to 35% versus 18% positive, while February had equal positive and negative counts.

evidence.label: Charge report, 13 December 2019
evidence.text: ITV reported that Flack was charged with assault by beating on 13 December after an incident the previous day. The allegation was not a conviction.

evidence.label: Flack steps down from Love Island, 17 December 2019
evidence.text: ITV reported that Flack stood down from the upcoming series after the charge. Her statement said reports about her private life did not reflect events as she understood them; she said she would cooperate with authorities and could not comment further during the legal process. ITV accepted her decision.

evidence.label: Laura Whitmore named host, 20 December 2019
evidence.text: ITV announced Laura Whitmore as the replacement host after Flack stepped down; Whitmore described Flack as a friend and said she wished circumstances were better.

evidence.label: Not-guilty plea reported, 24 December 2019
evidence.text: ITV’s 24 December report states Flack pleaded not guilty at Highbury Corner Magistrates’ Court on 23 December. She remained on bail ahead of a trial then scheduled for March. The same report records her statement that scrutiny and speculation were difficult to face alone and that she was taking time away to feel better.

evidence.label: Independent report of Sun story and its removal (secondary)
evidence.text: The Independent reported the Sun story and later removal. It remains secondary evidence; the original Sun H1, kicker, and times are now directly visible in the separate archived Sun record.

evidence.label: Removal reported after the window
evidence.text: The Guardian reported on 15 February that the Sun page had been replaced by a legal removal notice. The Guardian could not establish the exact removal time; this later removal report is distinct from the original Sun article and its 14 February archive capture.

evidence.label: Public debate about press coverage
evidence.text: The Guardian reported criticism of tabloid coverage and recorded The Sun executive editor Dan Wootton’s public claim that ITV had failed to stand by Flack. The response and criticism are viewpoints, not evidence that coverage caused her death.

evidence.label: Public Strain
evidence.text: Reports her public response and stated distress after the hearing.

evidence.label: LBC report on Burton’s response to circulated bedroom photographs (1 January 2020)
evidence.text: This verified LBC headline reports that Burton denied the blood shown on a stained bed was his. It reports his response; it does not identify whose blood it was or independently establish the photographs’ origin.

evidence.label: Relationship Rumour
evidence.text: Reports Flack's objection to gossip coverage amid breakup reports.

evidence.label: Original Sun Valentine-card article (14 February 2020 snapshot)
evidence.text: Archived Sun page displayed H1: “Brutal Caroline Flack Valentine’s Day card mocks troubled star with ‘I’ll f***ing lamp you’ message”; separate kicker: “NO FLACKS GIVEN”. First published 14 Feb 2020, 12:02; updated 14 Feb 2020, 12:33; Wayback capture 2020-02-14T20:52:41Z. The underlying assault allegation remained unresolved; this evidence does not establish motive or causation.

evidence.label: Court Eve Distress
evidence.text: Reports a distinct pre-hearing statement, one day before the plea hearing.

evidence.label: The Sun item, 2019-12-13 (recovered sample)
evidence.text: H1: “Why was Caroline Flack arrested, will she go to prison and what actually happened?”; page: “Published: 14:06, 13 Dec 2019”. The Sun page was read in the browser on 2026-10-14. Its displayed H1 and Published timestamp were visible. No pre-death capture was retrieved, so this confirms current page metadata and the publisher's first-publication date, not independently the exact headline as displayed in 2019.

evidence.label: The Sun item, 2019-12-14 (recovered sample)
evidence.text: H1 begins: “Caroline Flack’s boyfriend hit with phone after she saw flirty texts”; page: “Published: 23:03, 14 Dec 2019”. The live publisher page was read in the browser on 2026-10-14; displayed H1, byline, and Published timestamp were visible. The account of the alleged argument is attributed in the article to a source; it is not independently established by this record. No pre-death capture was retrieved, so historical H1 wording remains unconfirmed.

evidence.label: The Sun item, 2019-12-16 (recovered sample)

evidence.label: The Sun item, 2019-12-17 (recovered sample)
evidence.text: H1 begins: “Caroline Flack’s gone into ‘self-destruct mode’”; page: “Published: 13:08, 17 Dec 2019”. The Sun page was read in the browser on 2026-10-14; its displayed H1, byline, and Published timestamp were visible. The headline attributes its characterization to unnamed 'pals'; it is not a clinical assessment. No pre-death capture was retrieved, so exact headline-at-publication is not independently preserved.

evidence.label: The Sun item, 2019-12-17 (recovered sample)
evidence.text: Kicker: “FLACK OFF”; H1: “Devastated Caroline Flack quits Love Island after assault charge”; Published: “10:42, 17 Dec 2019”. The live Sun publisher page was read in the browser on 2026-10-14; displayed H1, kicker, and Published timestamp were visible. The page states she announced she was standing down. No pre-death capture was retrieved, so the displayed H1 is not independently preserved as of first publication.

evidence.label: The Sun item, 2019-12-17 (recovered sample)
evidence.text: Kicker: “FLACK SACK & WHACK”; H1 begins: “ITV stars furious as Caroline Flack forced to quit Love Island”; page: “17 Dec 2019, 22:31”; updated “18 Dec 2019, 7:57”. The live publisher page and a rendered Wayback snapshot were both read. The page identifies first publication at 22:31 on 17 Dec and an update at 07:57 on 18 Dec 2019; the retrieved archive capture is later, on 30 Oct 2020. The displayed kicker is 'FLACK SACK & WHACK'; it is distinct from the H1. The snapshot does not itself prove the headline was unchanged after 2019.

evidence.label: MailOnline (Daily Mail) item, 2019-12-13 (recovered sample)
evidence.text: H2 begins: “Caroline Flack, 40, is arrested and charged with assault by beating”; page: “PUBLISHED: 08:16 EST, 13 December 2019”. A rendered Wayback snapshot was read in the browser. It displays this headline as the article H2 and gives PUBLISHED 08:16 EST, 13 Dec 2019 and UPDATED 22:59 EST, 13 Dec 2019. The capture is from 2020-12-13, well after the death coverage; it verifies the dated page metadata and captured text, not a contemporaneous 2019 snapshot. The publisher domain was blocked by the web retrieval tool; browser/archive content was not obtained by bypassing access controls.

evidence.label: Media source · ITV News · 2019-12-17
evidence.text: ITV reported that Flack would stand down from the next Love Island series after being charged; it quoted her statement that media reports had not reflected matters as they were and that she could not comment further while proceedings continued. Date basis: hosting_page_publication. Web publication time is evidenced; it is not an airing time. ITV's page attributes Flack's statement to her Instagram account, but this record is ITV's report, not an independently inspected original Instagram post.

evidence.label: Media source · ITV News · 2019-12-23
evidence.text: The report covered Flack's first court hearing, where she pleaded not guilty; it also relayed arguments made by the prosecution and defence at the hearing. Date basis: hosting_page_publication. Courtroom claims are reported allegations, not findings. The online publication time does not prove when the clip aired on television; do not treat web page plus embedded clip as two items.

evidence.label: Restraint after a death · Editorial
evidence.text: Urges restraint in reporting after Flack’s death, arguing that public interest does not justify sensational detail or disregard for relatives and vulnerable readers. Institutional position, not evidence of an owner’s private views or direction. The linked page may have changed since first publication. This is aftermath after the 14 February cutoff, not evidence of pre-death coverage or a cause of death.

publicContext.intro: Caroline Flack was a television presenter. After a criminal charge in December 2019, reports followed her court appearance, her departure from Love Island and her private life. She died in February 2020. This timeline ends before her death: you judge the reporting choices using the events and information available then.
publicContext.allegationResponse: The case does not establish what caused her death. The 99 Sun print-story figure covers a separate six-month analysis; it is not the number of headlines in this dated online-inclusive sample. The charge remained unresolved after a not-guilty plea in this window.

Pleaded not guilty; bail conditions remained; trial set for March 2020
Christmas message: said she was taking a social-media break and was not going to be silenced
Lewis Burton denied that blood shown in bedroom photos was his.
Relationship-breakup reports were challenged; Flack objected to her family's life being treated as entertainment or gossip

researchUpdate.summary: Integrated eight URL-distinct dated publisher records (seven Sun, one MailOnline), corrected h21 to the directly retrieved original Sun Valentine page, and recalculated the full recovered sample and four-outlet chart.
researchUpdate.headlineDateTreatment: Displayed headline, page first-publication time, update time and archive capture time are separate fields. Current Sun page metadata confirms current displayed H1/date but not necessarily the H1 at first publication. Later snapshots preserve captured text but are not contemporaneous proof.
archiveChecks: Direct same-day Wayback Valentine capture opened from the Guardian removal report: capture 2020-02-14T20:52:41Z; original Sun URL, H1, separate kicker, first-publication and update times visible.
Wayback snapshots were read for Sun ITV-comparison (2020-10-30) and MailOnline charge item (2020-12-13); both captures postdate publication and are labelled accordingly.
The Sun page 10551729 returned its unavailable page with no readable article/capture verified; it was not counted.

CDX discovery remained incomplete: Sun wildcard query empty; DailyMail query returned 403 authorization required. Wayback availability requests returned 429 during this investigation; repeated requests were stopped. No host/proxy change or access-control bypass was attempted.
researchUpdate.searchLimits: No exhaustive archive coverage or full publication census. Several Sun pages were verified from current live publisher metadata, without pre-death snapshots; their original-display wording is not independently preserved. MailOnline was read through a later Wayback capture because web retrieval was robots-blocked. No causal or intent inference is supported.

title: Raheem Sterling: tattoo scrutiny and the 2018 challenge about racialised football coverage
subject: Raheem Sterling: tattoo scrutiny and the 2018 challenge about racialised football coverage

source.name: Recovered headline sample
source.scopeNote: Fixed window 2018-05-28 through 2018-12-16 inclusive. The retained sample contains 15 dated Sterling headline records across four playable desks (The Guardian, The Independent, The Sun and BBC Sport). It includes two direct Guardian pages dated 29 May, one Sun print headline reproduced by the Guardian, one Sun web page dated 28 May, and one BBC Sport page. The Foden MailOnline page is comparator context only and excluded because it is about Foden; the January Adarabioyo comparator remains unretrieved and outside this window. Missing records are unknown, not zero; this is not a census and does not establish motive, harm or causation.
source.sampleNote: 15 records retained for Sterling. The Sun print item is a contemporaneous secondary reproduction, while its 28 May web story is a direct original publisher page. Four desks are playable; Foden's verified MailOnline story is source-linked comparison context, not a Sterling row.

evidence.label: publisher report
evidence.text: Sterling explained that the rifle tattoo had a personal meaning connected to his father being killed by a gun; he said he understood why an uncontextualized image could prompt criticism. The tattoo is not evidence of promoting gun use.

evidence.label: publisher report / response
evidence.text: Sterling compared two MailOnline headlines about young Manchester City players buying homes for their mothers, alleging that wording cast Black player Tosin Adarabioyo in a more negative light than white player Phil Foden. The publisher and commentators disputed claims of intent; do not convert comparison into proof of motive or causal link to alleged stadium abuse.

evidence.label: reported allegation
evidence.text: Police and Chelsea said they were investigating an alleged racist incident at Stamford Bridge; no arrest was reported in this account. Allegation and investigation are not an adjudicated finding.

evidence.label: Public-interest chronology: 2018-05-29
evidence.text: The Sun foregrounded an image of Sterling’s rifle tattoo; Sterling publicly explained it as connected to his father’s killing and said it was unfinished. The explanation changes the context needed to assess criticism; it does not settle every reader’s view of the imagery.

evidence.label: Public-interest chronology: 2018-06-01
evidence.text: England manager Gareth Southgate publicly supported Sterling and described the tattoo’s meaning as individual. A relevant institutional response adds context, not a finding about press motive.

evidence.label: Southgate response reported 1 June 2018
evidence.text: The audited publisher headline reports Gareth Southgate’s support for Sterling over the tattoo controversy.

evidence.label: Publisher response reported 11 December 2018
evidence.text: Audited publisher headline reports the response to criticism of coverage.

evidence.label: The Sun print headline (reproduced contemporaneously)
evidence.text: Contemporaneous Guardian report published 29 May 2018 states The Sun placed the tattoo image on that day's front page and gives the reproduced headline. The Independent's contemporaneous page independently says the story was on Tuesday's front page, but the Sun page itself was not recovered. Record this as a print edition, not a Sun web article. Headline and date evidence: Guardian page: first published 29 May 2018; it attributes the front-page wording to The Sun.

evidence.label: The Guardian news
evidence.text: Publisher page shows the exact headline and first-publication timestamp (29 May 2018, 11:10 CEST). It reports the FA response, Sterling's explanation, and The Sun front page. It is a distinct story missing from the current Guardian records. Headline and date evidence: Publisher H1 and first-published time are visible on the Guardian page, lines 49 and 57.

evidence.label: The Guardian comment
evidence.text: Publisher page shows exact headline and first-publication time (29 May 2018, 17:23 CEST). This is a comment/analysis item, not straight news; it quotes the reproduced Sun headline and reviews earlier coverage. Keep genre explicit. Headline and date evidence: Publisher H1 and first-published time are visible on the Guardian page, lines 49 and 57.

evidence.label: BBC Sport news-web
evidence.text: Direct BBC Sport article opened in ordinary browser UI; displayed H1 and Published date visible. The body reports FA support, Sterling's explanation, and references The Sun's front-page story. This is an additional publisher's own contemporaneous web report, not a print item. Headline and date evidence: BBC Sport H1: “Raheem Sterling: FA shows support after gun tattoo row.” Displayed publication date: 29 May 2018.

evidence.label: The Sun news-web
evidence.text: Direct original Sun article opened in ordinary browser UI; page H1 and published time visible, with body describing initial publication of the tattoo story. This is The Sun's web article dated 28 May, separate from the 29 May print front-page item already documented. Headline and date evidence: The Sun H1: “England ace Raheem Sterling sparks fury by unveiling M16 assault rifle tattoo on his leg.” Displayed publication time: 21:57, 28 May 2018.

evidence.label: MailOnline comparator page, outside subject attribution
evidence.text: The publisher page directly verifies the exact Foden headline and first publication on 4 October 2018 (updated 5 October). This is a story about Phil Foden, not Raheem Sterling; exclude it from the Sterling headline corpus. It is cited only because Sterling later compared it with the Adarabioyo story.

evidence.label: Media source · BBC Sport · 2018-12-09
evidence.text: BBC Sport published a page reporting Sterling's criticism of newspaper portrayals of young Black footballers and embedded a clip in which Ian Wright comments on criticism of Sterling. Date basis: hosting_page_publication. This verifies BBC's online publication and embedded clip caption, not a separate broadcast airing or the original upload date of the video. BBC reports Sterling's social post; the article is not itself Sterling's original post.

evidence.label: A reported leader response · Leader column, attributed by contemporaneous reporting
evidence.text: Denied racial bias. This link is the report, not the original leader. Its exact original title and publication metadata remain unverified. It evidences an attributed institutional defence, not proof of motive, truth or owner direction.

evidence.label: A sports writer reconsiders the coverage · Comment · Dave Kidd
evidence.text: Kidd welcomed Sterling’s challenge and acknowledged unfair reporting. He defended the tattoo as a legitimate topic while saying he would not have made it the front-page lead. He called for greater diversity and dialogue in sports journalism. This is the named writer’s argument, not an unsigned leader or a statement by the owner. Its online date precedes the next day’s reported leader; disagreement is documented, but private editorial discussions are not reconstructed here.

evidence.label: Lineker challenges the coverage
evidence.text: Praises Sterling’s work ethic and condemns his treatment, linking Keyworth’s thread. Displayed timezone is not stated. Likes and reposts observed years later cannot establish the audience or pace of circulation during the 2018 window.

evidence.label: A headline-comparison thread
evidence.text: JOE reports a thread collecting negative coverage and describes it as widely shared that morning. The date plotted is the report’s date, not a verified thread publication date. The full thread and screenshots were not recovered; no article list or reach number is inferred.

briefing.title: A fictional desk defence of its sampled coverage

paragraphs.text: In this fictional exercise, two retained items cover the tattoo story. One is a web report published on 28 May; the other is a 29 May print headline reproduced in a contemporaneous report. The web page is directly available; the print item has no recovered scan or original page. These are separate formats and dates, not duplicate copies of one article.

The strongest challenge is the emphasis on anger around the tattoo, which could invite judgment before readers reach Sterling’s explanation. A responsible account should place his explanation near the top: he connected the image to his father’s killing and said he would never touch a gun. Readers need not approve of the tattoo, but this context matters to how they understand it.

Our defence is that the image and public criticism were already a live World Cup story, and the web report included campaigners’ objections and Sterling’s response. We should still examine whether the headline gave too much weight to outrage and whether the opening gave enough weight to his explanation. That is the strongest question these records raise about our choices.

The limit is clear: two items cannot show all our coverage, readers’ reactions, or whether a headline influenced the later alleged abuse. The print wording is a contemporaneous reproduction, not an original page. The comparison involving other players cannot establish our motive or prove a causal link. We should identify each format and source precisely, and accept that this sample cannot settle fairness across the wider press.

briefing.title: A fictional desk defence of its sampled coverage

paragraphs.text: In this fictional exercise, our one retained report was published on 29 May, as the tattoo story drew criticism. Its headline foregrounds the Football Association’s support after the row, while the article reports Sterling’s explanation and the FA response. We would defend covering a public controversy when an England player and the governing body had addressed it.

The strongest challenge is whether the headline gave readers enough context. A reference to a ‘gun tattoo row’ can leave the image and conflict in the foreground, even when the article explains Sterling’s personal reason. We should ask whether the headline and opening made that explanation visible, rather than assuming that context later in the article corrects the first impression.

Our answer is that reporting the FA’s support added a distinct, attributable development. We should include Sterling’s account that the tattoo connected to his father’s killing, and avoid presenting the image as evidence that he supported gun use. Readers can understand both the criticism and his explanation without being asked to hold one view of the tattoo.

The specific limit is that one dated page is one record in an incomplete sample. It cannot establish how this desk covered the story on other days, how its audience reacted, or whether its wording was fair across all formats. The later allegation about abuse and debate about newspaper framing are separate developments; this report cannot establish motive or causation. We would make those boundaries clear whenever we cite the sample.

The October Foden story is directly verified but excluded because it concerns Foden, not Sterling; the January Adarabioyo original page was not retrieved and remains an out-of-window Guardian-referenced comparator. publicContext.intro: Raheem Sterling was an England and Manchester City footballer whose tattoo, spending and experiences of racism drew coverage in 2018. An alleged racist-abuse incident on 8 December was followed by his public criticism of newspaper framing on 9 December. Examine whether coverage investigated racism, repeated personal judgment or helped readers understand the wider issue.
publicContext.allegationResponse: The recovered sample includes criticism of newspaper coverage as well as reports about Sterling. It does not measure every article about him.

searchLimitations: No original The Sun page-image, scan, or article URL for the May 2018 front page was retrieved. Available evidence is contemporary reproduction by other publishers; the Sun print headline is kept distinct from their own web headlines.
The 2018-12-09 alleged racist abuse remains a contemporaneous allegation under investigation in the Guardian report; no adjudicated finding is offered here.
No race-motive claim is supported by counting or comparing these headlines alone.

title: Meghan Markle: private-letter publication and the 2019 media wave
subject: Meghan Markle: private-letter publication and the 2019 media wave

source.name: Recovered headline sample
source.scopeNote: Fixed window 2019-02-06 through 2019-02-23 inclusive. Ten dated records: four Guardian publisher pages, five Mail/MailOnline article titles transcribed in paragraph 6 of the 2020 High Court judgment, and one directly verified People context page dated 6 February. Three playable desks remain; People is context-only, not a fourth chart desk. Court records two print headlines and three MailOnline web headlines, all dated 10 February 2019. Secondary commentary also gives 9 February; retain the court date pending original timestamp evidence. The sample does not establish overall volume or trends.
source.sampleNote: 10 records including one People context-only publisher page; chart retains three desks and nine playable/countable records. Five Mail/MailOnline titles are court-transcribed, not direct publisher page recoveries. Print/web distinction preserved; no private letter text.

paragraphs.text: We would defend the 23 February report as coverage of a legal threat, not a court ruling. The five challenged titles documented by the court belong to another publisher and are not a complete media count.

briefing.title: A fictional desk defence of its sampled coverage

paragraphs.text: Our strongest defence is that these updates followed distinct public developments rather than simply repeating a missing-person alert. On 8 February, a private search specialist described an area his team had checked; that was an attributed observation, not a police conclusion. The recovered 14 February page records two arrests on suspicion of malicious communications and the reported procedural status. On 15 February, police addressed speculation and disclosed limited personal information. The archive confirms the 14 February account; later police material explains the official position. Those dates and sources belong in the story because readers needed to distinguish a search account, an arrest update and an official briefing.

That defence has limits. Former specialists’ theories and police descriptions can attract attention without resolving what happened. A careful report should label expert comment as opinion, explain the basis for police statements, and avoid turning absence of information into a claim. Later identification or review findings cannot be projected backwards as facts known to readers that week. The sample does not show every editorial decision, every contact with the family or the full wording and prominence of every item. It also cannot establish that coverage caused harm. Our case is about what these dated items added, not a claim that every choice was justified.

Compared with the other selected reporting, this strand is strongest where it gives a verifiable new status and weakest where commentary risks outrunning evidence. The family’s later request to stop speculation is a necessary counterpoint; it should prompt restraint, not be treated as proof of a specific breach. The archive lookup was partial, and a failed check of one incorrect URL says nothing about other snapshots. These records support a limited defence of timely updates, alongside a clear obligation to correct uncertainty and avoid repeating unsupported theories.

briefing.title: A fictional desk defence of its sampled coverage

paragraphs.text: The clearest defence is that these reports tracked several genuinely different developments. On 16 February, the family asked people to stop speculation while the search was still under way. On 19 February, police said a body had been recovered but identification was pending. On 20 February, police confirmed the identity and the family issued a further statement criticizing speculation and media approaches. Then, on 21 February, Ofcom said it had written to two broadcasters seeking explanations. A recovery, an identification, a family response and a regulator’s request each changed what the public could responsibly know. Reporting them on separate dates helps readers follow that sequence rather than collapse it into one event.

The counterargument is serious: the family had asked for privacy and criticized direct approaches, so news value does not excuse intrusive contact or unnecessary personal detail. The Ofcom letter was an information request, not a decision that rules had been breached. The family’s criticism is their account and must remain attributed; it is not itself a regulatory finding. Later reviews also need their own dates and sources. A headline can record timing and emphasis, but this sample cannot reveal every approach made, the full prominence of each report, or the experience of the family.

Against the other selected coverage, this sequence has public value when it clearly marks what changed between 19, 20 and 21 February. It becomes repetitive if it merely recycles grief or speculation without new verified information. The strongest editorial defence is therefore narrow: establish the recovery, wait for formal identification, carry the family’s response with care, and describe Ofcom’s next step precisely. These records support that chronology, not a blanket claim that every story or contact was justified, and they provide no basis for claiming that reporting caused the death.

briefing.title: A fictional desk defence of its sampled coverage

paragraphs.text: A reasonable defence is that these selected items moved between different kinds of information: a 9 February search update, former detectives’ recommendations published early on 15 February, criticism of police disclosure, and later oversight news. The expert article appeared at 06:50 GMT, before the police press conference that day, so it should be understood as commentary in the developing search, not a response to the briefing. On 22 February, the review announcement and the IOPC referral concerned separate processes. That distinction matters: a review being commissioned is a new procedural development, but it is not a final finding about police conduct.

The counterargument is that lists of possible clues can amplify speculation, particularly when a family is living through a search and has asked for privacy. Former detectives’ suggestions do not establish that police missed a line of inquiry or that any theory was true. Nor does later oversight prove that every earlier report was wrong. A careful defence must acknowledge the duty to minimize personal detail, label professional commentary, and separate it from confirmed fact. The selected records cannot show the full article treatment, all editorial choices or how readers responded, and they do not establish harm or causation.

Compared with straight police updates, the expert piece offered interpretation rather than a new verified fact; compared with later oversight coverage, the 22 February announcement marked a process beginning, not its conclusion. The fairest account recognizes both public interest in examining search decisions and the risk of presenting conjecture as discovery. Subsequent official findings must be identified as retrospective and were unavailable to readers in this window. Four sampled records are too few to characterize the whole desk. They support a limited defence of covering distinct stages, paired with restraint where additional detail would only feed uncertainty.

publicContext.intro: Nicola Bulley disappeared in Lancashire in January 2023. Public coverage moved from search updates and speculation to scrutiny of police communication and later oversight. A body was recovered on 19 February and identified as Bulley on 20 February. Consider when reporting added verified public information and whose decisions warranted scrutiny.
publicContext.allegationResponse: Use minimal personal detail. Attribute family criticism and distinguish it from regulatory findings. The College review is retrospective; this sample does not attribute Bulley’s death to reporting.

sequence.text: A private search specialist said his team had not located Bulley in a specified section of river.
Police said two people had been arrested on suspicion of malicious communications; the reported bail and custody statuses were provisional procedural states.
The Independent published former-detective commentary at 06:50 GMT, before the police press conference; this was not a police update.
At a press conference police described Bulley’s risk classification and addressed speculation, followed by disclosure of limited personal information.
Police announced recovery of a body from the River Wyre; formal identification had not yet taken place.
Police confirmed the recovered body was Nicola Bulley; the family statement criticized speculation and media approaches and asked for privacy.
Ofcom said it had written to Sky and ITV seeking explanations after the family’s complaints; this was a request for information, not a breach finding.
The PCC announced a College of Policing review; the force also referred its prior contact to the IOPC, which later confirmed the referral date and investigation scope.

events.label: Christopher Jefferies was arrested on suspicion of Joanna Yeates’s murder; arrest was not proof or a charge.

briefing.title: A fictional desk defence of its sampled coverage

paragraphs.text: The selected reports can be defended as coverage of separate steps, not one continuing allegation presented as fact. On 1 January, the report said Jefferies had been released from custody on police bail while the investigation continued. In May, the Attorney General announced planned contempt proceedings; in June, a hearing preview recorded that the publishers denied liability. On 29 July, the High Court made a finding about specified articles, and a separate page reproduced the judgment. A November report then covered Jefferies’s evidence to the Leveson Inquiry. These are distinct procedural events. The two July pages are distinct pieces of journalism, but they describe one court decision, not two independent findings.

The main counterargument is that the press had a duty to report a murder investigation, but that duty did not turn suspicion into proof. Jefferies was arrested, not charged, and the contemporaneous Attorney General warning was not itself a later court judgment. The contempt decision applied to identified publications; it does not classify every story in this sample. November testimony is a retrospective account, valuable but not necessarily information readers possessed during the arrest period. The defence must preserve those distinctions and avoid using the later ruling to imply that every newsroom knew the eventual findings at the time.

Compared with the print headlines preserved in the inquiry evidence, these later reports supply dated procedural context and response. Compared with the judgment reproduction, the news article summarizes rather than creates the legal outcome. Their public value lies in explaining what changed and who said so. The record remains incomplete: a bounded sample cannot establish all coverage, newsroom intent, the effect on Jefferies, or causation. A defensible account acknowledges both the legitimate interest in reporting a major investigation and the specific legal limits later applied to particular articles.

briefing.title: A fictional desk defence of its sampled coverage

paragraphs.text: Evidence for this desk is narrow: two dated print headlines reproduced in Christopher Jefferies’s Leveson witness-statement exhibits. They show the words readers could see and when those editions appeared, which makes them relevant to a discussion of reporting during an active murder investigation. They are not recovered web pages, and they do not provide the full articles, surrounding page, editorial process or any response that may have appeared elsewhere. A fair defence can explain the public interest in timely reporting and the importance of recording what was published, while being candid that these exhibits alone cannot supply the complete reporting context.

The strongest counterargument is that Jefferies was arrested on suspicion, not charged or convicted, and headlines can create a firm impression before evidence is tested. The High Court later found contempt in relation to specified articles published on 31 December and 1 January. That is a concrete legal outcome and must be faced directly. The exhibit headlines are not, by themselves, the full reasoning for the ruling, and the finding should not be stretched to every item from this publisher or the wider press. Nor should retrospective knowledge be presented as what editors or readers necessarily knew on publication day.

Compared with the contemporaneous print evidence, the later official summary and judgment provide the legal assessment that the headlines could not. Compared with other sampled outlets, this record contains fewer items and less original article material, so it cannot support a broad claim about a whole newsroom. The appropriate defence is limited: publishing on a matter of urgent public interest is not automatically contempt, but the court’s finding governs the specified articles. The responsible conclusion acknowledges both the reporting context and the failure identified by the court, without claiming intent, audience harm or consequences beyond the evidence.

briefing.title: A fictional desk defence of its sampled coverage

paragraphs.text: This sample contains a mix of forms that should not be treated as interchangeable. The 1 February item is an editorial arguing against naming uncharged people, so it is opinion rather than a legal change. On 8 March, a news report said police had confirmed that Jefferies’s bail conditions had ended. A July article reported the High Court contempt decision, and a November article covered his evidence at Leveson. These items add a public debate, a status update, a court outcome and a retrospective account. Their value depends on making clear which kind of statement each one is and what date it belongs to.

The counterargument concerns the March headline’s phrase “formally cleared.” The article reported police confirmation that bail conditions had ended; the phrase must not be recast as an acquittal or a charge decision. Jefferies had never been charged. The later judicial review judgment supports the fact that he was innocent, but that later legal record does not mean every reader knew the full story in March. Likewise, his November account is attributable testimony, not independent proof of every allegation. A careful defence recognizes how compressed headlines can overstate what the underlying event establishes.

Compared with outlets represented chiefly by reproduced print headlines, this sample includes an editorial and later reporting, but it remains only four selected records. The July report describes one specific contempt ruling concerning identified articles; it is not a finding against every publication in the wider sample. The November story adds Jefferies’s retrospective perspective, which should be distinguished from contemporaneous knowledge. Taken together, the items show changing public information and debate. They do not establish the desk’s intent, the total effect on Jefferies, or that any single report caused an outcome.

briefing.title: A fictional desk defence of its sampled coverage

paragraphs.text: The two available records for this desk are print headlines dated 31 December and 1 January, reproduced in the Leveson evidence. They document contemporaneous wording during an active murder investigation and are relevant to understanding what readers encountered. They are not original online pages, and the exhibits do not reproduce full articles or all surrounding context. A limited defence can point to the public interest in reporting an urgent investigation and to the value of preserving exact print evidence. It cannot claim that headlines alone tell us what the newsroom knew, what qualifications appeared in the articles, or how the stories were handled across all editions.

The central counterargument is that Jefferies had been arrested on suspicion but not charged, and sensational wording can invite readers to treat suspicion as guilt. The High Court later found contempt in relation to a specified article published on 1 January. That finding must be stated plainly, while keeping its scope exact: it concerned identified material, not every Sun story or every report in the wider case. It is also retrospective. The court’s later assessment should not be described as knowledge necessarily available at the time, and the arrest itself was never proof of guilt.

Compared with later news reports and the court record, the print exhibits preserve wording but offer less context. The official summary and judgment establish the specific outcome; the print headlines establish what was published. Neither source should be asked to prove more than it can. A responsible desk defence can acknowledge a legitimate public-interest subject while accepting that the eventual contempt finding applies to the stated article. This small sample cannot establish motive, audience effect, total coverage or causation, and it cannot be used to label every article as unlawful.

He was released from custody on police bail on 1 January and was never charged. The Independent reported on 8 March that his bail conditions had ended. Later contempt findings applied to specified Daily Mirror and Sun articles; they do not classify all coverage.
publicContext.allegationResponse: Early Daily Mirror and Sun headline evidence is reproduced print material from Jefferies’s Leveson witness statement. The original digital publisher pages were not recovered in this research. Keep arrest, custody release, release from bail conditions, court findings and retrospective testimony separate.

sequence.text: Christopher Jefferies was arrested on suspicion of Joanna Yeates’s murder; arrest was not proof or a charge.
Jefferies was released from custody on police bail; the investigation continued and he was not yet free of bail conditions.
The Independent published an editorial calling for limits on naming uncharged people and criticizing the press treatment; this was commentary, not a legal change.
The Independent reported police confirmation that Jefferies’s bail conditions had ended. This is the report date; the article’s “formally cleared” phrasing is not an acquittal or a charge decision.
The Guardian reported that the Attorney General planned to launch contempt proceedings the next day; permission was granted on 12 May. This was a procedural step, not a finding.
The Guardian previewed the scheduled contempt hearing and reported that both publishers denied liability.
The High Court found the Daily Mirror and The Sun in contempt over specified articles; the decision does not classify every item in the coverage.
Jefferies gave evidence to the Leveson Inquiry about his account of the press coverage; this testimony is retrospective.
